OVERVIEW

[1] XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXXand XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellants), citizens of Iran, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated May 16, 2022, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.

[2] The Appellants detail their allegations in their Basis of Claim (BOC) forms1 and subsequent amendments and additions.2 During the first hearing of their claim for refugee protection, the Principal Appellant and her children claimed they faced persecution in Iran because of the threats they had received from an alleged Sepah member named XXXX XXXX, who threatened the family in Canada and Iran. Their claim was refused on the grounds of credibility and was appealed. Their appeal was allowed and returned to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted panel. Prior to the Appellants' second hearing in 2022, a new set of allegations were made. The Appellants now allege that they fear return to Iran based on their conversion to Christianity. The Appellants claim that if they were to return to Iran, they would be at risk of persecution from both XXXX and the Iranian regime.

[3] The RPD had numerous credibility concerns with the Appellants' claims. The Appellants argue that the RPD:
a. Erred in the manner in which they conducted the hearing;
b. Erred in their credibility assessment; and
c. Erred in failing to consider the supporting documentary evidence before it.3

[4] In reviewing this decision, I have considered and applied the Chairperson's Guideline 4: Gender Considerations in Proceedings Before the Immigration and Refugee Board (the Guideline)4 as it relates to the Principal Appellant's allegations and appeal.
New Evidence

[5] The Appellants submitted five new pieces of evidence:
1) A letter from the XXXX XXXX XXXX Church dated XXXX XXXX, 2022;5
2) Certificate of Baptism for XXXX XXXX dated XXXX XXXX, 2022;6
3) Certificate of Baptism XXXX XXXX XXXX dated XXXX XXXX, 2022;7
4) Photographs dated XXXX XXXX, 2020;8
5) Photographs dated XXXX XXXX, 2022.9

[6] Subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) provides that the Appellants may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claims or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

[7] The second step in the analysis for new evidence is to consider it in relation to the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh.10 In Singh, the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) held that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) should assess the admissibility of the new evidence for its credibility, relevance, and newness. The RAD will therefore apply the Raza factors, minus the "materiality" factor, as this is to be assessed in light of subsection 110(6) of the IRPA only.

[8] In relation to item 4, I note that those photographs were taken of an event that took place prior to the rejection of the claim for protection and were part of the documentary evidence before the RPD. This item is not new and does not meet the statutory test and therefore is not accepted as new evidence.

[9] Items 1 to 3 and 5, are all dated in June or July of 2022, post-rejection of the claim and therefore could have not reasonably been expected to be provided prior to the RPD's decision in May of 2022. However, I do not find that these documents raise a new issue.

[10] The documents include a letter from the Appellants' church in British Columbia (BC), where they testified at the RPD hearing that they attended. There are also baptismal certificates for both XXXXand XXXX, as well as photographs. The children both testified at the hearing about their conversion to Christianity and what church they attended, they also spoke about their future plan for baptism. While no arguments have been made as to why I should accept these documents, I note that they address an issue that was already before the RPD, which is the Appellants' conversion to Christianity.

[11] Furthermore, the Appellants previously testified about their attendance at this church and that they were hopeful for baptism in the future. After reviewing these documents, I do not find there is any probative value in admitting them as new evidence. The documents deal with issues that were established before the RPD, that the Appellants attended a Christian church and that the children were hoping to be baptized. They do not, however, establish the intentions of the Appellants with regards to their religious pursuits or overcome the credibility concerns identified by the RPD relating to their alleged conversion. In my view, these items do not meet the jurisprudential test and are rejected as new evidence.

[12] Since I have not admitted any of the new documents into evidence, I do not have the authority to conduct an oral hearing under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.

ANALYSIS

[13] I agree with the RPD's credibility concerns and confirm the RPD's negative determination. I find that the determinative issue in this appeal is credibility.

[14] The RPD made numerous negative credibility findings, including but not limited to, delay in claim for protection, reavailment to Iran, significant changes in the Appellants' BOC forms, material omissions in the central allegations of the claim and vague, evasive and inconsistent testimony.
Hearing room conduct and interpretation

[15] The Appellants argue that the hearing was a "one way street conducted by the Member asking questions and the Appellants providing responses through an interpreter" and that the "questions was [sic] not clearly explained through translation."11 I have conducted an independent review of the transcript of the RPD hearing,12 and I disagree with the Appellants' characterization of the hearing. Indeed, the Member did conduct the hearing through an interpreter as required and did ask the Appellants questions.

argument_evidence.context_text: [16] I note that during the hearing there was two instances where the Associate Appellants interjected that the translator had paraphrased their mother's response to a question.
She noted that she welcomed interjection about incorrect interpretation, but that she could not accept testimony to complement their mother's testimony.
Again, the RPD Member was sensitive to the needs of the Principal Appellant, rephrased questions as required, and I do not find evidence that the RPD was "sarcastic"15 as alleged.
I find that the Member was impartial and did not conduct the hearing improperly.

I also note that the Member frequently rephrased questions as necessary, was sensitive to the Guideline and allowed for the Principal Appellant to testify about her allegations of sexual harassment and assault in private.
[18] I have conducted an independent review of the transcript, as well as the Record in this matter.
I find that the reasons, and the credibility findings therein, are correct.

subthemes.text:
[16] I note that during the hearing there was two instances where the Associate Appellants interjected that the translator had paraphrased their mother's response to a question. The Member explained that their complaint appeared to be about paraphrasing of what their mother said. She noted that she welcomed interjection about incorrect interpretation, but that she could not accept testimony to complement their mother's testimony.13 The Member then instructed the parties that they should provide short sentences and focus on answering the questions she asked.14

[17] I note that to date, there have been no allegations made to the RPD regarding the interpretation at the hearing that took place on May 3, 2022. There was no complaint made during the hearing, during submissions or prior to the decision being issued on May 16, 2022. The Appellants did not request an audit of the hearing's interpretation and they were instructed to interject at the hearing if there was a problem with the interpretation. I also note that the Member frequently rephrased questions as necessary, was sensitive to the Guideline and allowed for the Principal Appellant to testify about her allegations of sexual harassment and assault in private. I do not accept the allegation that the interpretation for the hearing was inadequate. The Appellants' have also argued that the RPD showed a reasonable apprehension of bias. I disagree. Again, the RPD Member was sensitive to the needs of the Principal Appellant, rephrased questions as required, and I do not find evidence that the RPD was "sarcastic"15 as alleged. I find that the Member was impartial and did not conduct the hearing improperly.
The RPD's credibility assessment

[18] I have conducted an independent review of the transcript, as well as the Record in this matter. I agree with each of the RPD credibility findings, for the same reasons provided by the RPD. These numerous credibility findings relate to material elements of the Appellants' claims and are consistent with the evidence. The Appellants argue that the RPD was responsible for their vague and evasive testimony, noting that the Member should be held accountable for rephrasing and asking clarifying questions; as well as erring by failing to "navigate the conversation between the Appellants and the interpreter in a manner that would allow for more specific responses."16 Having reviewed the transcript, I disagree. The RPD questioned the Appellants appropriately, put inconsistencies and omissions to them for clarification of their evidence and asked a number of clarifying questions throughout the hearing. The RPD's reasons are detailed and complete, they accurately reflect the testimony on the Record, and they are clear. I find that the reasons, and the credibility findings therein, are correct.

ANALYSIS

[13] I agree with the RPD's credibility concerns and confirm the RPD's negative determination. I find that the determinative issue in this appeal is credibility.

[14] The RPD made numerous negative credibility findings, including but not limited to, delay in claim for protection, reavailment to Iran, significant changes in the Appellants' BOC forms, material omissions in the central allegations of the claim and vague, evasive and inconsistent testimony.
Hearing room conduct and interpretation

[15] The Appellants argue that the hearing was a "one way street conducted by the Member asking questions and the Appellants providing responses through an interpreter" and that the "questions was [sic] not clearly explained through translation."11 I have conducted an independent review of the transcript of the RPD hearing,12 and I disagree with the Appellants' characterization of the hearing. Indeed, the Member did conduct the hearing through an interpreter as required and did ask the Appellants questions.

[16] I note that during the hearing there was two instances where the Associate Appellants interjected that the translator had paraphrased their mother's response to a question. The Member explained that their complaint appeared to be about paraphrasing of what their mother said. She noted that she welcomed interjection about incorrect interpretation, but that she could not accept testimony to complement their mother's testimony.13 The Member then instructed the parties that they should provide short sentences and focus on answering the questions she asked.14

[17] I note that to date, there have been no allegations made to the RPD regarding the interpretation at the hearing that took place on May 3, 2022. There was no complaint made during the hearing, during submissions or prior to the decision being issued on May 16, 2022. The Appellants did not request an audit of the hearing's interpretation and they were instructed to interject at the hearing if there was a problem with the interpretation. I also note that the Member frequently rephrased questions as necessary, was sensitive to the Guideline and allowed for the Principal Appellant to testify about her allegations of sexual harassment and assault in private. I do not accept the allegation that the interpretation for the hearing was inadequate. The Appellants' have also argued that the RPD showed a reasonable apprehension of bias. I disagree. Again, the RPD Member was sensitive to the needs of the Principal Appellant, rephrased questions as required, and I do not find evidence that the RPD was "sarcastic"15 as alleged. I find that the Member was impartial and did not conduct the hearing improperly.
The RPD's credibility assessment

[18] I have conducted an independent review of the transcript, as well as the Record in this matter. I agree with each of the RPD credibility findings, for the same reasons provided by the RPD. These numerous credibility findings relate to material elements of the Appellants' claims and are consistent with the evidence. The Appellants argue that the RPD was responsible for their vague and evasive testimony, noting that the Member should be held accountable for rephrasing and asking clarifying questions; as well as erring by failing to "navigate the conversation between the Appellants and the interpreter in a manner that would allow for more specific responses."16 Having reviewed the transcript, I disagree. The RPD questioned the Appellants appropriately, put inconsistencies and omissions to them for clarification of their evidence and asked a number of clarifying questions throughout the hearing. The RPD's reasons are detailed and complete, they accurately reflect the testimony on the Record, and they are clear. I find that the reasons, and the credibility findings therein, are correct.

[19] I also note that the RPD was respectful and acted appropriately when questioning around the issues of sexual assault and harassment. At the outset of the hearing, to ensure the comfort of the Principal Appellant, they made it clear that they would not be asking for too many details regarding the incidents with XXXX and would allow her to testify in private to ensure she was able to testify openly. The panel noted that there was a general lack of credibility with regards to the Principal Appellant, although accepted on a balance of probabilities that the Principal Appellant was a victim of sexual assault. The panel found however, that the allegation that the assault was at the hands of XXXX was not established by the objective documentary evidence that the Appellants' provided.

subthemes.text: [20] The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to properly assess the supporting documentary evidence in this case. I have reviewed the supporting documentary evidence that the Appellants supplied for their RPD claim. The RPD carefully considered the documentary evidence and put the material omissions and inconsistencies between the testimony and documents to the Appellants. The RPD noted that the documentary evidence in concert with the sworn testimony of the Appellants' created additional credibility concerns relating to material elements of the claim. I agree with the panel's assessment of the documentary evidence. They are inconsistent in respect to the Appellants' testimony. The RPD was correct in finding that the documentary evidence could not overcome the material omissions and inconsistencies relating to the central allegations of the claim. I agree with the findings of the RPD.

REASONS FOR DECISION AMENDED
OVERVIEW

[1] XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXXand XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellants), citizens of Iran, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated May 16, 2022, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.

[2] The Appellants detail their allegations in their Basis of Claim (BOC) forms1 and subsequent amendments and additions.2 During the first hearing of their claim for refugee protection, the Principal Appellant and her children claimed they faced persecution in Iran because of the threats they had received from an alleged Sepah member named XXXX XXXX, who threatened the family in Canada and Iran. Their claim was refused on the grounds of credibility and was appealed. Their appeal was allowed and returned to the RPD for redetermination by a differently constituted panel. Prior to the Appellants' second hearing in 2022, a new set of allegations were made. The Appellants now allege that they fear return to Iran based on their conversion to Christianity. The Appellants claim that if they were to return to Iran, they would be at risk of persecution from both XXXX and the Iranian regime.

[3] The RPD had numerous credibility concerns with the Appellants' claims. The Appellants argue that the RPD:
a. Erred in the manner in which they conducted the hearing;
b. Erred in their credibility assessment; and
c. Erred in failing to consider the supporting documentary evidence before it.3

[4] In reviewing this decision, I have considered and applied the Chairperson's Guideline 4: Gender Considerations in Proceedings Before the Immigration and Refugee Board (the Guideline)4 as it relates to the Principal Appellant's allegations and appeal.
New Evidence

[5] The Appellants submitted five new pieces of evidence:
1) A letter from the XXXX XXXX XXXX Church dated XXXX XXXX, 2022;5
2) Certificate of Baptism for XXXX XXXX dated XXXX XXXX, 2022;6
3) Certificate of Baptism XXXX XXXX XXXX dated XXXX XXXX, 2022;7
4) Photographs dated XXXX XXXX, 2020;8
5) Photographs dated XXXX XXXX, 2022.9

[6] Subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) provides that the Appellants may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claims or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

[7] The second step in the analysis for new evidence is to consider it in relation to the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh.10 In Singh, the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) held that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) should assess the admissibility of the new evidence for its credibility, relevance, and newness. The RAD will therefore apply the Raza factors, minus the "materiality" factor, as this is to be assessed in light of subsection 110(6) of the IRPA only.

[8] In relation to item 4, I note that those photographs were taken of an event that took place prior to the rejection of the claim for protection and were part of the documentary evidence before the RPD. This item is not new and does not meet the statutory test and therefore is not accepted as new evidence.

[9] Items 1 to 3 and 5, are all dated in June or July of 2022, post-rejection of the claim and therefore could have not reasonably been expected to be provided prior to the RPD's decision in May of 2022. However, I do not find that these documents raise a new issue.

[10] The documents include a letter from the Appellants' church in British Columbia (BC), where they testified at the RPD hearing that they attended. There are also baptismal certificates for both XXXXand XXXX, as well as photographs. The children both testified at the hearing about their conversion to Christianity and what church they attended, they also spoke about their future plan for baptism. While no arguments have been made as to why I should accept these documents, I note that they address an issue that was already before the RPD, which is the Appellants' conversion to Christianity.

[11] Furthermore, the Appellants previously testified about their attendance at this church and that they were hopeful for baptism in the future. After reviewing these documents, I do not find there is any probative value in admitting them as new evidence. The documents deal with issues that were established before the RPD, that the Appellants attended a Christian church and that the children were hoping to be baptized. They do not, however, establish the intentions of the Appellants with regards to their religious pursuits or overcome the credibility concerns identified by the RPD relating to their alleged conversion. In my view, these items do not meet the jurisprudential test and are rejected as new evidence.
[12] Since I have not admitted any of the new documents into evidence, I do not have the authority to conduct an oral hearing under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.
ANALYSIS
[13] I agree with the RPD's credibility concerns and confirm the RPD's negative determination. I find that the determinative issue in this appeal is credibility.

[14] The RPD made numerous negative credibility findings, including but not limited to, delay in claim for protection, reavailment to Iran, significant changes in the Appellants' BOC forms, material omissions in the central allegations of the claim and vague, evasive and inconsistent testimony.
Hearing room conduct and interpretation

[15] The Appellants argue that the hearing was a "one way street conducted by the Member asking questions and the Appellants providing responses through an interpreter" and that the "questions was [sic] not clearly explained through translation."11 I have conducted an independent review of the transcript of the RPD hearing,12 and I disagree with the Appellants' characterization of the hearing. Indeed, the Member did conduct the hearing through an interpreter as required and did ask the Appellants questions.

[16] I note that during the hearing there was two instances where the Associate Appellants interjected that the translator had paraphrased their mother's response to a question. The Member explained that their complaint appeared to be about paraphrasing of what their mother said. She noted that she welcomed interjection about incorrect interpretation, but that she could not accept testimony to complement their mother's testimony.13 The Member then instructed the parties that they should provide short sentences and focus on answering the questions she asked.14

[17] I note that to date, there have been no allegations made to the RPD regarding the interpretation at the hearing that took place on May 3, 2022. There was no complaint made during the hearing, during submissions or prior to the decision being issued on May 16, 2022. The Appellants did not request an audit of the hearing's interpretation and they were instructed to interject at the hearing if there was a problem with the interpretation. I also note that the Member frequently rephrased questions as necessary, was sensitive to the Guideline and allowed for the Principal Appellant to testify about her allegations of sexual harassment and assault in private. I do not accept the allegation that the interpretation for the hearing was inadequate. The Appellants' have also argued that the RPD showed a reasonable apprehension of bias. I disagree. Again, the RPD Member was sensitive to the needs of the Principal Appellant, rephrased questions as required, and I do not find evidence that the RPD was "sarcastic"15 as alleged. I find that the Member was impartial and did not conduct the hearing improperly.
The RPD's credibility assessment

[18] I have conducted an independent review of the transcript, as well as the Record in this matter. I agree with each of the RPD credibility findings, for the same reasons provided by the RPD. These numerous credibility findings relate to material elements of the Appellants' claims and are consistent with the evidence. The Appellants argue that the RPD was responsible for their vague and evasive testimony, noting that the Member should be held accountable for rephrasing and asking clarifying questions; as well as erring by failing to "navigate the conversation between the Appellants and the interpreter in a manner that would allow for more specific responses."16 Having reviewed the transcript, I disagree. The RPD questioned the Appellants appropriately, put inconsistencies and omissions to them for clarification of their evidence and asked a number of clarifying questions throughout the hearing. The RPD's reasons are detailed and complete, they accurately reflect the testimony on the Record, and they are clear. I find that the reasons, and the credibility findings therein, are correct.

[19] I also note that the RPD was respectful and acted appropriately when questioning around the issues of sexual assault and harassment. At the outset of the hearing, to ensure the comfort of the Principal Appellant, they made it clear that they would not be asking for too many details regarding the incidents with XXXX and would allow her to testify in private to ensure she was able to testify openly. The panel noted that there was a general lack of credibility with regards to the Principal Appellant, although accepted on a balance of probabilities that the Principal Appellant was a victim of sexual assault. The panel found however, that the allegation that the assault was at the hands of XXXX was not established by the objective documentary evidence that the Appellants' provided.
Supporting documentary evidence

[20] The Appellants argue that the RPD failed to properly assess the supporting documentary evidence in this case. I have reviewed the supporting documentary evidence that the Appellants supplied for their RPD claim. The RPD carefully considered the documentary evidence and put the material omissions and inconsistencies between the testimony and documents to the Appellants. The RPD noted that the documentary evidence in concert with the sworn testimony of the Appellants' created additional credibility concerns relating to material elements of the claim. I agree with the panel's assessment of the documentary evidence. They are inconsistent in respect to the Appellants' testimony. The RPD was correct in finding that the documentary evidence could not overcome the material omissions and inconsistencies relating to the central allegations of the claim. I agree with the findings of the RPD.
CONCLUSION

[21] The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
